articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign
articles.content_orig:
Estimated read time: 4-5 minutes
DUBLIN, Ohio — Wendy's rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low and didn't take into account the company's long-term earnings potential under its new CEO.
The Dublin, Ohio-based burger chain also said Thursday that its board had adopted a "poison pill" plan designed to make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results. Wright, who is the fourth CEO to lead Wendy's since 2024, was previously the president and CEO of Potbelly. He has also held senior leadership roles at Wendy's, Checkers and Domino's Pizza.
"We're confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy's to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value," Wright said.
Shares rose less than 1% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance in the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it "substantially undervalues" the company.
Wendy's shareholder rights plan — commonly known as a "poison pill" plan — grants all shareholders except a hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares and dilute the hostile bidder's ownership stake. It is automatically triggered if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said.
Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. Peltz served as chairman of Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024. His son Bradley Peltz still serves on the company's board and is a Wendy's franchisee.
Dine Brands, the parent company of Applebee's and IHOP, adopted a similar one-year poison pill plan last week to fend off a takeover bid by two investment firms.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy's is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic "Where's the beef?" ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy's fell behind. Wendy's share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.
The industry has also been seeing lower U.S. traffic, especially from lower-income customers, as high gas prices and affordability concerns eat into household budgets. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
Wendy's has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy's filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy's restaurants in 15 states.
Under Wright, Wendy's has launched a turnaround plan dubbed "Dave's Way," which calls for improving food quality, more distinctive marketing and improved digital ordering and restaurant operations.
Wright said Thursday that Wendy's has begun testing quality improvements, including thicker and crispier bacon, creamier Frosties and whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches. The company is removing lower-volume items from its menus to reduce complexity in its kitchens and making breakfast optional, allowing franchisees to focus on their most profitable times of day.
Wendy's on Thursday reported revenue of $547 million in the July-September period. That was better than the $531 million Wall Street had forecast, according to analysts polled by FactSet. Wendy's same-store sales, or sales at locations open at least a year, fell 5.2%, which was also better than the 6.4% drop analysts forecast.
Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.

Quantum computing stocks have spent the past month giving back ground, and IonQ ( NYSE:IONQ ) sits near the center of the slide. IonQ stock is down 32% over the past month, recently trading at $29.70. Shares are up 5% from the prior close, a modest bounce after a steep decline.
The selloff has hit the whole group, which suggests IonQ is moving with its sector as risk appetite for speculative technology cools off. Rigetti Computing ( NASDAQ:RGTI ) stock is down 28% over the past month to $10.94. Meanwhile, D-Wave Quantum ( NASDAQ:QBTS ) shares have slid 35% over the past month to $10.23, a steeper fall than IonQ's.
For IonQ, the pullback has come even after a strong second quarter and a string of acquisitions, leaving investors to figure out whether the slide points to lasting problems at IonQ or a correction across the whole sector.
IonQ's Q2 2026 revenue rose 287% year over year to a record $80.1 million in results released on August 5. Excluding acquisitions, IonQ grew 132% organically. Management's 2026 revenue outlook for IonQ now includes the SkyWater Technology acquisition, which closed July 31, and calls for $450 million to $460 million. That $1.8 billion deal brought a semiconductor foundry in-house. On the hardware side, IonQ is developing its 256-qubit Superion system, and management plans to start commissioning those systems in 2027.
In September, IonQ announced a quantum computing partnership with NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA ). A pending acquisition of Elisity would add to IonQ's quantum security business.
Wall Street remains mostly bullish on IonQ, with 11 Buy ratings and one Hold over the past three months. The average analyst price target on IonQ stands at $65.45.
IonQ's Q2 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) came in at negative $120.3 million, and its operating expenses reached $417.3 million. Under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), IonQ's net loss hit $1.9 billion, mostly because of a $1.6 billion non-cash warrant revaluation the company disclosed.
All the acquisitions make IonQ's organic growth harder to judge. Folding in SkyWater could also put pressure on IonQ's margins. On the August call, IonQ CFO Inder Singh said, "So don't draw a straight line up into the right from any one of the data points."
The commercial return for IonQ still depends on how well it executes and how fast customers adopt quantum tools. Quantum stocks have also been volatile. As the past month's drops at Rigetti and D-Wave show, that volatility is exactly why speculative names like these belong in a small, rules-based allocation of a portfolio (we laid out the sizing and exit rules in a free guide here).
IonQ builds trapped-ion quantum computers and sells a full platform covering computing, networking, sensing and security, while Rigetti uses superconducting qubits at a smaller scale and D-Wave works on quantum annealing, which suits a different class of problems.
With SkyWater and Nexus Photonics, IonQ now handles chip manufacturing and integrated photonics itself, a vertically integrated model its two peers don't share.
Q3 2026 results from IonQ arrive on November 5, after the market close. Analysts expect a loss of $0.34 per share, compared with a $3.58 loss a year earlier. Investors will be watching whether organic revenue keeps growing apart from acquired sales and whether SkyWater weighs on margins.
Bulls have record revenue, a bigger outlook and an active hardware roadmap on their side. IonQ's bears point to deep losses, heavy spending and a sector subject to sharp swings. Whether IonQ looks hopeless or ready for a rebound depends on which of those lists the coming quarters back up.
Investors can watch for updates on the Superion timeline and on SkyWater's margins in the upcoming report. Cautious traders may want to see how the debate over IonQ's margins settles before drawing any firm conclusions.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
President Donald Trump's celebration of Wall Street's highs aged rather poorly. Less than 24 hours after boasting about Americans' retirement accounts going "through the roof," the S&P 500 plunged as much as 3.8% Thursday, bringing emergency trading halts into the conversation.
The selloff prompted traders to monitor the market's circuit-breaker thresholds, which can temporarily shut down trading across U.S. stock exchanges when losses become too severe. The S&P 500 would need to fall another 3.2 percentage points from its decline to trigger the first emergency halt.
The timing is particularly awkward for Trump, who has repeatedly pointed to stock market performance as evidence of his administration's economic success.
"Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof," Trump wrote Wednesday on his Truth Social account. He closed the message with "Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP."
Wall Street had rallied Wednesday following the Democratic Party's sweeping midterm election victories. The S&P 500 gained 1.6%, its strongest daily performance in three months, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped more than 1,500 points to 53.361 points.
Thursday's losses erase that rally in a single session, with technology stocks taking the biggest beating.
The U.S. stock market has three emergency thresholds designed to slow panic selling. These mechanisms, known as circuit breakers, automatically suspend trading when the S&P 500 falls by a specified percentage from its previous closing price.
The first threshold is a 7% decline, corresponding to an S&P 500 level of 7,150.41 points for Thursday's session. Reaching that level before 3:25 p.m. ET would trigger a 15-minute halt across US equity markets.
The circuit breaker level is located in the following chart's blue line
A 13% decline, or 6,689.09 points, would trigger another 15-minute suspension. The most severe threshold comes at 20%, or 6,150.89 points, which would shut down trading for the remainder of the day.
Under the New York Stock Exchange's rules, the first two circuit breakers stop applying at 3:25 p.m. ET, while the 20% threshold remains active throughout the session.
The rules apply to the entire U.S. equity market, not just stocks included in the S&P 500. A market-wide halt would also suspend trading in companies listed on the Nasdaq and other US exchanges.
The technology sector was particularly hard hit as investors continued digesting the consequences of Tuesday's election results. At around 11 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite had fallen nearly 5%, while the S&P 500 was down 3.2%.
Nvidia lost more than 6%, while the broader semiconductor index plunged nearly 11%. Companies involved in building AI infrastructure were also under pressure as investors worried that Democratic victories could bring stricter oversight of data-center construction.
"We suspect there is going to be some scrutiny on this aggressive AI buildout," Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank, told Reuters .
The selloff also spilled into cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin fell below $76,000, wiping out its post-election recovery as approximately $428 million in leveraged crypto long positions were liquidated within an hour, as Decrypt reported earlier today.
Stocks also faced pressure from persistent inflation concerns and uncertainty over the Federal Reserve's next interest-rate decision. Investors are awaiting Friday's October employment report, which could provide further clues about the direction of monetary policy.
Despite Thursday's sharp losses, the S&P 500 had not reached its first market-wide circuit breaker at the time of this report.

US stocks plunged on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday's post-election rally.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 4.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5.5%, with the tech-heavy index closing in correction territory.
The Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) fell 6.3%, erasing $2.3 trillion in market value.

Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.
Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil ( BZ=F ) prices traded around $98 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude ( CL=F ) stood at $90 per barrel.
A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.
On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy ( DUK ), Airbnb ( ABNB ), and Lumentum ( LITE ), among others, report results.
Stocks plunged on Thursday amid carnage in the AI trade on Wall Street.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) plunged 4.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 5.5%, closing in correction territory.
Chip stocks took the brunt of the beating, with severe losses for Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and AMD ( AMD ), among others. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank 12%.
Institutional investors dumped the top performers of 2026 to lock in gains. Retail traders followed suit, unloading $265 million of equities in their biggest selling day since 2020.
Meanwhile, regulatory concerns weighed on AI data center build-out stocks. SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) also plummeted over fears of regulatory hurdles following Democrats' congressional victory.
Retail investors are dumping US stocks at a pace not seen since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, breaking with their typical market-down-day habit of "buying the dip."
Everyday investors sold a net $358 million in individual US stocks on Thursday as of 2:58 p.m. ET, according to Vanda Research, putting them on track for their biggest single-day net selling spree since March 17, 2020, when retail investors pulled $502 million from individual stocks.
"This is what we would call a total capitulation by retail investors," Viraj Patel, global macro strategist at Vanda Research, said in emailed comments.
The selling marks a departure from retail investors' tendency to scoop up shares when markets tumble. Vanda said there were "no signs of buying the dip" in individual stocks, though some investors continued purchasing leveraged exchange-traded funds such as the ProShares UltraPro QQQ ( TQQQ ) and Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares ( SOXL ).
Patel added that the retreat echoed a broader "buyers' strike" among institutional investors alongside forced selling by systematic and leveraged investment strategies.
The AI trade's marquee stocks got clobbered on Thursday, sparking warnings on Wall Street of an institutional shakeout as investors move to lock in gains.
"They're shooting the generals," wrote Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott on Thursday.
The unwinding of the 2026 popular thematic stocks has been "wildly acute" for more than a month, the strategist noted. The primary catalyst isn't about a sudden deterioration in fundamentals, but a frantic dash by hedge funds to lock in their profits before the end of the year.
"Single-name stock moves are absolutely BONKERS," wrote McElligott. "The Momentum/High Sharpe unwind has been so substantial that we are approaching the dreaded 'Round Trip' levels in some trades."
The carnage has hit semiconductor and hardware stocks particularly hard. Shares of Lam Research ( LRCX ) are down 36% over the past month. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) has shed 30% over the past month, while AMD ( AMD ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are also down 22% and 15%, respectively, over the same period.
Goldman Sachs ( GS ) promoted 109 employees to its coveted partnership on Thursday, its largest class since 2010, as the Wall Street giant elevated record numbers of asset managers and engineers to its senior ranks.
The new class is nearly 15% larger than in 2024 when Goldman named 95 partners, according to a statement from the bank.
Of the 109 new partners, 60 work in Goldman's investment banking and trading division, while 33 are in Asset & Wealth Management. The firm also promoted 13 engineers.
In a departure from previous years, a Goldman executive declined to disclose the gender and racial makeup of the new class, citing changes in the legal environment. The executive added that with the latest round of promotions, the firm has more than 100 female partners.
Partnership status at Goldman is considered highly exclusive. The firm promotes new partners every two years. The promotion comes with higher compensation and additional financial benefits, including opportunities to invest in the firm's private funds.
Once promotions take effect in January, Goldman will have a little over 500 partners, an executive said, amounting to roughly 1% of Goldman's workforce.
It's a bad day for the stock market.
Major indexes are falling Thursday, with technology stocks leading the sell-off and semiconductor shares among the biggest decliners.
But one rough session doesn't necessarily amount to what investors deem a correction.
A correction generally refers to a decline of at least 10% from a recent high in a stock, index, or other asset. It is typically seen as a meaningful pullback, but one that stops short of a bear market, which is commonly defined as a drop of 20% or more.
That distinction matters after Wednesday's sharp rally. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) and the narrower Nasdaq-100 are each on pace to close Thursday in correction territory, as is the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ).
Meanwhile, the Dow and S&P 500 (down 3% and 4% from yesterday) aren't close to correction territory.
The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) just fell below its 200-day moving average, according to AlphaSpace data (see chart below).
Several individual names, such as Nvidia ( NVDA ), also broke through their 200-day averages, a technical indicator that tracks a stock's long-term trend.
"I think this has been brewing for quite some so much time because there have been so many investors poking at this perceived AI bubble, almost hoping it's going to burst, Hennion & Walsh chief investment officer Kevin Mahn told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang.
"So this type of volatility shouldn't necessarily come as a surprise to anybody … but there's going to be more choppiness ahead," Mahn added.

articles.title_orig: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles broke out in Nantes and authorities arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by an estimated 575,000 people – remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike was organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors were impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
Our live coverage of the protests in France has ended for the day. Read more on the topic here
At least 448 people have been detained during the nationwide protests in France, the country’s Interior Ministry said, though that is a fraction of the estimated 575,000 who took part.
The ministry revised down its count of protesters, from the 600,000 it reported earlier today .
There were about 65,000 protesters in Paris alone, the ministry said.
The marches across the country were largely peaceful and proceeded without major incidents, the ministry said. There were some clashes between police and “groups of radical and far-left activists” in places like Rennes, Nantes, Lyon and Marseille, it said.
Firefighters responded to 86 fires, including one at a school common room that was destroyed in Toulouse, it said. An effigy of a police riot officer was set on fire in Strasbourg.
Hundreds of thousands of people are protesting across France today, but it’s a movement that grew out of protests that happened two months ago.
In September, students and teachers at a high school in the Parisian suburbs went on strike, demanding more staff and resources. Their demands were met and the strike ended – but it lit a spark that soon caught nationwide.
The movement has since swelled into a collective cry of anger, bringing together groups with different grievances, capturing widespread discontent over affordability, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide, and a deep desire for social and political change.
No longer confined to students, the movement has drawn in trade unions and yellow vest protesters, who are voicing frustrations over the cost of living and calling for French President Emmanuel Macron to go. The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions.
With so many causes now fueling the protests, the anger is unlikely to subside anytime soon.
And with France heading into a deeply divisive presidential election in April , the stakes are only getting higher.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, claimed at the end of October that “legitimate social grievances have, yet again, been held hostage by the far left.” Her hard-left rival, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has repeatedly defended the students’ right to protest.
The skyrocketing cost of living in France is one of the factors driving this wave of protests as anxieties around low wages, high prices and the state of public services explode onto the streets.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.

articles.title_orig: Gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. So why are fuel costs falling?
articles.title_zh: Gas prices could soon dip below $4 a gallon. So why are fuel costs falling?
articles.content_orig:
Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.
Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving, he said.
Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was largely due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Other factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.
The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.
Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual.
"Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. "A more normal markup would be 40 cents a gallon, and that means that even if futures prices and physical markets hang around present levels, we should see lower pump prices for the foreseeable future."
The Trump administration has used various tools to ease gas prices. That includes expanding access to tax-free red-dyed diesel , opening the door to Russian diesel imports , and waiving what's known as the Jones Act , a federal statute that requires goods shipped between U.S. ports to be moved on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.
The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.
Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.
The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.
Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

The IRS has released the 2027 standard deduction amounts you'll use for your 2027 tax return — and they're higher than ever.
The federal tax agency adjusts these amounts for each filing status every year. Since these adjustments are based on inflation, the standard deduction is higher for 2027 than in recent years.
Knowing the standard deduction for your status can help you determine whether you should plan to itemize or claim the standard deduction next year.

Taxpayers age 65 and older, as well as those who are blind, can claim an additional standard deduction . For 2027, that additional amount is $1,700 ($2,100 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse).
Those eligible can add the extra standard deduction to the regular amount for their filing status. A single taxpayer 65 or older (or who is blind) can claim a total standard deduction of $18,700 on their 2027 federal tax return.
Additionally, as Kiplinger has reported, the 2025 Trump tax bill introduced a new bonus standard deduction of $6,000 for those age 65 and older.
This can be added to the 2027 standard deduction for each eligible individual and can be claimed by those who itemize.
However, the "bonus" amount is temporary and phases out for incomes above certain thresholds.
Your standard deduction amount might differ if you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal tax return.
The 2027 standard deduction for dependents is limited to either $1,400 or the sum of $500 and the dependent's earned income, whichever is greater.
Note: The standard deduction for dependents cannot exceed the regular standard deduction for your filing status, even if your earned income is higher than the basic standard deduction amount.
Given the new senior bonus deduction, the existing extra standard deduction for those over age 65, and changes to the base standard deduction, the highest possible 2027 standard deduction amount is a whopping $48,600.
That amount is for married couples filing jointly who are both age 65 or older, qualify for the bonus deduction, and can claim the extra standard deduction for both spouses.
For more information on how to calculate your total standard deduction, see: The Extra Standard Deduction for People Age 65 and Older .

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark-Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 4, 2026.
As Democrats are celebrating a historic blue wave , eyes are on the Senate race in deep-red Mississippi, where the Democratic candidate led the Republican incumbent by a razor-thin margin of 1,138 votes as of Wednesday evening.
The Associated Press has not yet called the race because it is so close, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom ahead by about 0.1%—he has so far earned 49% of the vote compared to Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 48.9%, with 96% of votes counted. It’s a stunning nail-biter of a race that, in the weeks leading up to Election Day, polls had suggested would likely be won by the Republican incumbent by a narrow margin.
“I can’t recall the last time it’s been this close for a statewide Senate contest—or a statewide election in general,” says Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University. “It’s unprecedented for [Mississippi] to be this competitive for Democrats particularly, certainly in the last 40 years.”
Read More: What Democrats’ Midterm Gains Reveal About Trump’s Voter Coalition
Political experts say it could take a few days before the outcome of the race becomes clear.
If Colom, a district attorney, wins the race, it would be the first time that Mississippi voters have elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. Senate since 1982. A Democratic victory would also be a remarkable shift in a state that President Donald Trump won by a nearly 23-point margin just two years ago.
Such an upset would cap off a string of staggering victories for Democrats, who have so far flipped seven seats in the upper chamber in this year’s midterm elections, including in other staunchly red states like Texas and South Carolina .
Both candidates appeared to be optimistic that the election would ultimately go their way, though they also acknowledged that the race is still too close to call. Colom said in a statement early Wednesday morning, “I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat.”
“The results are all trending in our direction,” Colom said in a speech to his supporters on Election Night. “The reality is, though, we’re not going to get the results tonight. I’m excited about our momentum, I’m excited about where we are.”
Speaking to a crowd of her supporters on Election Night , Hyde-Smith said she was confident that she would hold her seat in the upper chamber.
“We still don’t have all the votes in, so we’re not calling all of it tonight, but we’re in a very good lead and I assure you, I will continue to be your U.S. Senator,” she said .
When asked about Hyde-Smith’s speech at a press conference on Wednesday, Colom replied , “Bless her heart.”
It is possible that the winner of the Senate contest may not be determined until the end of the week—or even next week.
The state has five business days after Election Day to count affidavit ballots. An individual would turn in such a ballot, which is also called a provisional ballot, in a situation in which they believe they’re eligible and registered to vote but are unable to cast a standard ballot—for instance, if their name is not in their local polling place’s records. These votes are only counted once election workers verify the individual’s information. Mississippi also permits mail-in ballots that arrive within five days after Election Day, so long as they were postmarked by Election Day, to be counted.
All this means that it’s possible the race may not be called until a week after Election Day, says Emily Ommundsen, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.
“Because of the razor-thin margins we currently see, I don’t expect any results to be called before then,” Ommundsen says.
The tight race in Mississippi is one of many that illustrate the extremely challenging political environment Republicans have faced this year.
Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in midterm elections, and that pressure on Republicans was compounded in this election cycle because of historically low approval for Trump driven in large part by the economy, as well as the war in Iran.
Ommundsen says that, while ballots are still being counted, the result in Mississippi, so far, “is consistent with trends that we saw nationally.”
“Nearly all counties that had a Senate election on the ballot moved towards the left compared to how they voted in 2024,” she says, though she notes that there are some exceptions. “Mississippi just happens to be one of those elections that was closer and perhaps more ripe for a flip.”
Hitefield likens this year’s midterms to “a referendum on the President,” adding that “Democrats were turning out to oppose the President and to oppose the President’s policies.”
But he cautions that the close contest in Mississippi is not necessarily a sign that the deep-red state is turning blue or even purple. It’s possible, he says, that Republican voters didn’t cast their ballots for a Democrat, and instead stayed home.
“I wouldn’t necessarily read in, long story short, to Mississippi becoming a Georgia—you know, being a fully competitive every election state,” Hitefield says. “But I think it’s certainly moving toward a state that you shouldn’t sleep on when it comes to electoral competitiveness.”
Hitefield also says that there’s a lot of “voter apathy” within the Republican party with regards to Hyde-Smith, and she hasn’t performed as well as Mississippi’s other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, in past elections. Wicker won his re-election bid in 2024 by a more than 25-point margin . Hyde-Smith, meanwhile, won her re-election fight in 2020 by about 10 points .
Hitefield adds that Hyde-Smith had some “gaffes” during the campaign, when she made some remarks about the rising cost of living that some voters felt were dismissive. For instance, when asked about soaring costs, including beef prices, during an interview with WLOX in February, Hyde-Smith applauded the passing of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill and went on to say, “It is on everybody’s mind. It is certainly me at my house. And you know, you have so many proteins to choose from. And all commodities go through peaks and valleys.”
National polling ahead of Election Day indicated that an overwhelming majority of American voters felt that the economy was a crucial issue for them heading into this year’s midterms.
Colom’s campaign jumped on Hyde-Smith’s remark, releasing an ad in which people objected to Hyde-Smith’s comment, including one who said in the video, “Pick another protein? Sh**, I’d rather pick another Senator instead.” The ad racked up more than 7.5 million views on Colom’s X account .
Ommundsen points out that Hyde-Smith didn’t make many public campaign appearances in this year’s election cycle; one of the few appearances the Senator made was last week, when she gave very brief remarks at a rally the President held for her in Mississippi.
Hitefield says Hyde-Smith didn’t “do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign” in this election cycle.
“I think that it was a real mistake by her campaign, regardless of what the outcome looks like at the end of this,” Hitefield says. “Even if she does win, she didn’t do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. I think that’s something [where] if she does win, she’ll need to think about, moving forward, how to strategize more effectively.”
Colom, on the other hand, ran a “successful campaign” and generated “so much voter excitement,” Hitefield says—so much so that it stirred “this groundswell of hopes within the Democratic party that this seat could be flipped.”

articles.title_orig: A Guide To China’s Expanding Fleet Of Military Helicopters
articles.title_zh: A Guide To China’s Expanding Fleet Of Military Helicopters
articles.content_orig:
China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA) operates an increasingly diverse fleet of helicopters spanning everything from basic pilot training and battlefield transport to airborne early warning, anti-submarine warfare, and dedicated attack missions.
The force reflects decades of development, often beginning with helicopters acquired from France and later produced under license, before transitioning to increasingly indigenous designs. The result is a mix of older aircraft that have undergone extensive modernization and newer platforms designed around the requirements of China’s expanding military, including its growing carrier and amphibious assault fleets .
The Z-8 family, originally derived from the Cold War-era French Super Frelon , is a particularly good example of this evolution. It has spawned a wide range of specialized variants, including search and rescue, transport, electronic warfare, and airborne command post helicopters. Meanwhile, the Z-20 — frequently alluded to as a Sikorsky S-70/H-60 clone — has emerged as a modern medium-lift platform with land-based, naval, and assault variants, while the Z-10 and newer Z-21 represent China’s growing emphasis on dedicated attack helicopters.
This guide examines the principal helicopter types operated by the PLA, their development, and the roles they are expected to perform.
At the same time, it should be noted that, as it now stands, the PLA remains heavily reliant on foreign-sourced helicopters for a wide variety of applications.
Russian-built helicopters give the PLA a mix of transport and specialized naval capabilities. The Mi-17/171 Hip family supports troop and cargo movement, search and rescue, special operations, and select high-altitude or mission-specific roles. At sea, the Ka-28 Helix provides anti-submarine warfare, while the Ka-31’s radar supports airborne fleet surveillance. These aircraft remain in service where their established capabilities continue to meet operational needs. However, they are increasingly supplemented by Chinese designs, including certain designs that have been tailored to provide direct replacements.
The HC-120 is a light utility helicopter derived from the EC120, a design co-developed by China, France, and Singapore during the 1990s. The type entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2005, providing a modern platform for primary helicopter training and replacing the aging SA316 Alouette III in that role.
The HC-120 is powered by a single Turbomeca Arrius 2F turboshaft engine. Its introduction represented an important step in modernizing the Army Aviation training fleet, giving pilots experience with a more contemporary helicopter before transitioning to larger operational types.
The Z-11 is a light utility helicopter developed by Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation (CHAIC) and the 602 Research Institute. The design is based on the French AS350BA Écureuil , examples of which were acquired for Army Aviation.
Deliveries of the Z-11 to Army Aviation began in 1998. The helicopter is powered by a single WZ-8D turboshaft engine and is primarily used for training, liaison, and other light utility duties.
A scout and armed reconnaissance derivative, designated as the Z-11WB, was developed with a nose-mounted electro-optical (EO) turret and external weapon pylons capable of carrying rockets, missiles, and gun pods. Its operational status remains unclear, although it provided the basis for the unarmed Z-11A training helicopter used by the Army Aviation Academy.
The Z-8 was developed from the French SA321Ja Super Frelon, 13 examples of which China purchased during the late 1970s. Changhe Aircraft Industries Corporation subsequently developed an indigenous version during the 1980s.
Powered by three WZ-6 turboshaft engines, the original Z-8 became the foundation for a broad family of helicopters serving the PLA Navy (PLAN), Army Aviation, and People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF).
The Z-8J is the naval transport variant, with a boat-like hull. For anti-submarine warfare (ASW) missions, the helicopter can be equipped with a surface-search radar, a French HS-12 dipping sonar, and Whitehead A244S or ET52 torpedoes.
Several specialized derivatives were developed from the Z-8J:
The Z-8J and Z-8JH have both been used aboard Chinese aircraft carriers, providing transport and support capabilities for embarked naval forces.
The Z-8C represents a substantially improved successor to the original naval Z-8J series. The helicopter was first reported in 2016 and incorporates a number of changes intended to improve its performance and operational versatility.
The most visible differences include a redesigned nose with a chin-mounted weather radar, a FLIR turret, and a pilot night-vision system (PNVS) mounted above the cockpit. A searchlight is also fitted, while the longer engine compartment accommodates the WZ-6C turboshaft engine.
The Z-8C is operated by the PLA Marine Corps, while the Z-8CJ serves as a training variant with the Naval Aviation University.
The helicopter has become a principal transport platform for the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, supporting the movement of troops and equipment between ships and shore.
The PLAAF introduced the Z-8K in 2007 as a dedicated search-and-rescue helicopter. The related Z-8KA is configured for combat search and rescue (CSAR), including the recovery of personnel from hostile or contested environments.
Both versions feature a FLIR turret, searchlight, radar-warning receiver (RWR), chaff and flare dispensers, and a rescue hoist. Some aircraft are also equipped with small terrain-following radars beneath the nose to support low-level operations.
Selected helicopters have received satellite communications (SATCOM) antennas on top of the tail boom, improving their communications capabilities over longer distances.
A further derivative, the Z-8KH, was developed for the PLAAF garrison stationed in Hong Kong. This version is distinguished by chaff and flare dispensers integrated into its flotation equipment.
The Z-8B entered service with PLA Army Aviation in 2011 as an improved transport helicopter. It shares several characteristics with the Z-8KH but lacks the latter’s flotation equipment.
The Z-8B incorporates a glass cockpit and has become a major component of the Army Aviation transport fleet. Some aircraft have subsequently had flotation equipment reinstalled, reflecting the type’s continuing evolution.
An optional auxiliary fuel tank can be installed inside the cabin to extend its range. Other upgrades have included SATCOM antennas on the tail boom and, on some aircraft, WZ-6C engines, an EO turret, and a terrain-following radar beneath the nose.
A specialized operations variant has also been identified. These helicopters incorporate RWR, laser-warning receivers (LWR), and missile-approach warning system (MAWS) sensors, alongside flare dispensers and ceramic armor protection.
Lacking the boat-like hull of the Z-8B, the Z-8G is expected to replace that type in Army Aviation service. The helicopter was evaluated from 2014 and was specifically optimized for operations at high altitudes, including in Tibet.
Unlike earlier Z-8 variants, the initial Z-8G configuration uses imported Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6B-67A turboshaft engines. Its redesigned nose is longer and more aerodynamically efficient, while the glass cockpit and terrain-following radar support operations in demanding environments.
The helicopter also incorporates SATCOM and BeiDou/GPS antennas to improve communications and navigation during long-range missions.
Some Z-8Gs have been equipped for special operations, with combinations of MAWS, RWR, and LWR sensors mounted on the rear fuselage and sponsons, together with chaff and flare dispensers. Armor plates beneath the cockpit windows provide additional protection, and some aircraft carry a 12.7mm machine gun inside a cabin doorway.

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 27 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 27 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due to a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_orig: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.title_zh: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.content_orig:
Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing.
Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported , after they had drifted an estimated 3,355 miles east from the Federated States of Micronesia.
The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. The group had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo at the time, ABC reported.
A 10-day search covering 33,000 square miles followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said.
"Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care," the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email.
"Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them," the email added.
When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible.
A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island.
Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery.
"They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," she told the ABC.
The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. ABC said the group went missing after their boat was caught in a storm.
The governor of Micronesia's Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.
"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter.
"We continue to pray for their four companions," he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
There have been previous incidents where people have become lost at sea among the tiny island chains that stud the Pacific Ocean. An Australian man survived more than two months lost at sea in 2023 with his dog Bella after rough seas damaged their boat and its electronics system. Tim Shaddock, 51, had been traveling from Mexico to French Polynesia, but found himself drifting in the Pacific Ocean for more than two months. Shaddock and his canine companion survived by drinking rain water and eating raw fish that Shaddock caught, he said. They were spotted by a helicopter and rescued in July 2023.
Two American sailors and their two dogs were rescued after five months at sea in the Pacific in 2017. Jennifer Appel and Tasha Fuiaba were discovered 900 miles southeast of Japan by a Taiwanese fishing ship, the U.S. Navy said at the time. The vessel's engine died during bad weather, and they were unable to get to land using the ship's sails. The women said the boat drifted off course, and no ships were near enough to hear their distress calls. Water purifiers and a year's supply of food aboard the vessel kept them alive, the Navy said.
In 2024, three fishermen were stranded on a remote Micronesian island for more than a week . They were rescued after using palm leaves to spell out "HELP" in large letters on a beach.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla extend losses as midterm results cloud data center, merger outlook
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race.
Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla.
Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail.
“It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.”
Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit.
And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts.
SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans.
“I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose.
Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares.
The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 midterm elections
The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions.
Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches.
SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year.
How AI companies spent money on the midterms
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.”
Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.)
Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country.
Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads.
Musk bankrolling group using AI to attack Talarico on AI
“It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said.
Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said.
Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

iPhone Duo has only been available for a couple weeks, but Apple keeps improving the product with software enhancements. The latest arrives in the iOS 27.3 beta via a convenient keyboard update.
If you’re one of the fortunate early adopters who managed to get an iPhone Duo on or near launch day, you may have noticed that changes keep arriving via software updates.
iPhone Duo shipped with iOS 27.1, but just a few days later iOS 27.2 arrived and added Apple Pencil support and Edge Light for video calls.
Now just about one week later, the iOS 27.3 beta has introduced even more changes.
Reachability lets you slide outer display content to the left or right to make it more reachable. And as highlighted by Beta Profiles on X , the keyboard has gotten an improvement too.
iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z
The keyboard refresh with narrower keys and smaller font makes it easier than before to type on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen, especially one-handed.
It’s a subtle difference, but one that early testers have found a clear upgrade.
By combining keyboard changes with Reachability, iOS 27.3 offers a noteworthy improvement to the one-handed iPhone Duo experience.

articles.title_orig: Travelers busted at airport with over 3,000 tarantulas hidden away in their socks
articles.title_zh: Travelers busted at airport with over 3,000 tarantulas hidden away in their socks
articles.content_orig:
Forget snakes on a plane — Peru’s got spiders in socks.
Airport workers in Callao, Peru seized more than 3,000 tarantulas found stuffed inside socks in travelers’ luggage Tuesday.
The employees made the skin-crawling discovery inside the suitcases of three passengers at Jorge Chavez International Airport after recieving an anonymous tip.
The thousands of creepy crawlies were hidden inside 15 to 20 socks in each of the three travelers’ bags and included tarantulas in various stages of development, from eggs to young spiders to fully grown adults.
Officials believe the trio — two Germans and a Pole — planned to smuggle the eight-legged contraband to Germany to sell to arachnid lovers, according to SERFOR, Peru’s National Forestry and Wildlife Service.
Cora Suarez, a wildlife forestry control technician with SERFOR, explained that the hairy, venomous critters can be considered valuable.
“These species are attractive because of the colors, because of the size and, more than anything, because they can be intended for collectors,” Suarez said in Spanish.
All three passengers were detained by Peru’s environmental crimes police and now face prosecution by a specialized environmental prosecutor’s office.
Tuesday’s spider incident is not the first time a multi-legged stowaway has been the victim of an attempted smuggling on board a flight.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
In 2025, more than three dozen live beetles hidden in Japanese snacks were intercepted before they could be smuggled into the US.
Thirty-seven insects were discovered inside potato chips, chocolates and other snacks during a search as the air-cargo shipment arrived at Los Angeles International Airport from Japan, according to US Customs and Border Protection.
The agency noted that the insects are sought after by collectors and are likely worth around $1,500.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.title_zh: Outback Steakhouse franchisee files for bankruptcy after closures
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
A San Diego-based franchisee of Outback Steakhouse filed for bankruptcy on Monday, citing expensive food and labor costs and declining customer traffic.
Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, which operates 61 Outback Steakhouse locations mostly in California, said it has been struggling since the COVID-19 pandemic . The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Wilmington, Del., seeking relief from hundreds of millions in debt.
Cerca Trova also operates Outback Steakhouses in Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico but said that California’s minimum wage laws have made labor especially pricey for a majority of its restaurants.
More than half the company’s employees work in California, according to court documents.
California’s minimum wage, effective at the start of this year, is $16.90 per hour. Fast-food employers must pay a higher minimum wage of $20 per hour, but Outback Steakhouse is not classified as a fast-food establishment under the law.
Beverly Hills-based Fat Brands Inc. said in a statement that it filed for bankruptcy on Monday to restructure the debt it accumulated while expanding its company portfolio, citing ‘difficult and largely unforeseen’ market conditions.
“By 2026, the pressures on the business had converged,” Cerca Trova Chief Executive David Goronkin said in a court filing. “Guest traffic and earnings continued to decline, while food, labor, and other production costs continued to rise.”
The company’s debt has increased from $269 million in late 2020 to $449 million this year. It has between one and 49 creditors, court documents said.
Outback Steakhouse is not the only full-service casual dining restaurant to face challenges since the pandemic.
Red Lobster filed for bankruptcy in 2024, after its disastrous $20 all-you-can-eat shrimp deal . More recently, the Oprah-backed chain True Food Kitchen filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and closed three Southern California locations.
Inflation and economic pressure have led more Americans to eat at home or turn to fast food for a cheaper option, while the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic has curbed customers’ appetites.
The cost of beef has also been rising, up as much as 5% each year since 2022, Cerca Trova said in court filings.
Shares of Wendy’s jumped 15% at the opening bell after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the struggling burger chain
Cerca Trova was once the largest Outback Steakhouse franchisee, with 99 restaurants in 2018. As of June, there were 659 Outback Steakhouse locations nationwide, 544 owned and operated by the brand owner, Bloomin’ Brands. The rest are run by franchisees.
Bloomin’ Brands, headquartered in Tampa, Fla., also owns Bonefish Grill, Carrabba’s Italian Grill and Fleming’s Prime Steakhouse and Wine Bar.
The company has thrived this year despite pressures on the restaurant industry, with shares rising 60% since January. Shares fell Tuesday after Cerca Trova’s bankruptcy announcement and ended the day at $10.23, down 6.15%.  The company’s market value is nearly $879 million.
The Scottsdale, Ariz.-based health food chain True Food Kitchen announced it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Monday and has closed 12 locations.
Cerca Trova, also known as Out West Restaurant Group, proposed selling its assets to Bloomin’ Brands for $26.3 million unless a higher offer emerges during the bankruptcy process.
“This is an isolated situation involving the franchisee and does not affect Bloomin’ Brands’ corporate operations, financing, or liquidity,” Bloomin’ Brands spokesperson Elizabeth Daly said in an email. “Bloomin’ Brands is participating in the process as a stalking‑horse bidder to acquire Out West’s assets and seeking to support operational continuity and protect the brand while the court‑supervised process moves forward. ”
Cerca Trova could not be immediately reached for comment.
